topics.title: How the U.S. Constitution is wired
topics.dek: Three branches, the checks between them and how it gets amended

slides.h: Seven articles, written in a summer
slides.p: Fifty-five delegates met in Philadelphia from May to September 1787 to fix the failing Articles of Confederation and wrote a new government instead. The document has seven articles: the legislature, the executive, the courts, the states, amendments, federal supremacy and ratification. It took effect in 1789.

items: Articles of Confederation: no taxing power, no executive

slides.p: Congress makes law, controls spending and declares war. The President executes the law, commands the military, conducts foreign policy and appoints officials. The courts interpret the law and decide cases. Each is chosen differently, on a different clock, so no single election captures all three.

slides.h: Checks: each branch can stop the others
slides.p: The President vetoes bills; Congress overrides with two-thirds of both houses. The Senate confirms judges and treaties. Courts strike down laws and executive acts. Congress impeaches (House, majority) and removes (Senate, two-thirds) presidents and judges. Congress holds the purse; the President holds the pen.

slides.h: Judicial review wasn't in the text
slides.p: The Constitution doesn't say courts can strike down laws. Chief Justice John Marshall asserted it in Marbury v. Madison (1803) by voiding part of a statute, and the practice stuck. The Supreme Court's nine justices (a number set by Congress, not the Constitution) now decide the meaning of the whole document.

v.q: It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.
v.by: Chief Justice John Marshall, Marbury v. Madison, 1803

slides.p: Powers not given to the federal government are reserved to the states (Tenth Amendment). States run elections, schools, most policing and most courts; Washington handles defense, currency, interstate commerce and much else through the Commerce Clause. Federal law wins where the two conflict (Article VI).

slides.h: The Bill of Rights, and the rest of the amendments
slides.p: The first ten amendments (1791) list what government may not do: speech, press, religion, assembly, arms, searches, trials, punishments. Later amendments ended slavery (13th), guaranteed equal protection and due process against states (14th), and extended the vote by race (15th), sex (19th) and age 18 (26th).

slides.h: Amending it is hard on purpose
slides.p: Two-thirds of both houses of Congress propose, three-quarters of the states (38) ratify; or two-thirds of states call a convention, which has never happened. More than 11,000 amendments have been proposed; 27 have passed. The last substantive one, the 26th, was in 1971; the 27th, on congressional pay, took 203 years.

slides.h: Why the design looks the way it does
slides.p: The framers had read how the Roman Republic died and how Britain's king had been checked. They assumed ambition and designed so that, in Madison's phrase, ambition would counteract ambition. The result is slow by intent: big changes need broad, durable majorities across institutions elected on different timetables.

items: Separate powers, so no one body rules
Different electorates and terms, so no one election decides all
Rights that majorities can't vote away

quiz.q: Congress can override a presidential veto with…
a: A simple majority of the House
quiz.why: The veto check is itself checked by the override, which requires broad agreement in both chambers.

quiz.q: Judicial review, the power of courts to strike down laws…
a: Is spelled out in Article III
Was established by the Supreme Court in Marbury v. Madison (1803)
quiz.why: The text is silent; Marshall's opinion asserted the power and it has been accepted ever since.
Two-thirds of Congress proposes, 38 states ratify. The President has no formal role, which is why only 27 have passed.

take: Three branches with separate powers, elected on different clocks, each able to block the others.
Judicial review came from a case, not the text; federalism splits power with the states.
Amendment needs ⅔ of Congress and ¾ of the states, which is why there are only 27.

topics.title: GDP, inflation, unemployment: the numbers
topics.dek: What the headline statistics measure, who counts them and where they mislead

slides.h: GDP: everything made, added up once
slides.p: Gross domestic product is the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period, usually a quarter. 'Final' avoids double counting: the flour is in the bread. U.S. GDP is about $29 trillion a year; the growth rate you hear is quarter-over-quarter, annualised, adjusted for inflation.

Nominal GDP rises when prices rise even if nothing more is made. Real GDP strips out inflation to measure actual output. The same goes for wages: a 4 percent raise with 5 percent inflation is a 1 percent pay cut. Whenever a number spans years, ask whether it's real.

b: what was actually produced or bought

slides.p: The Bureau of Labor Statistics prices a basket of about 80,000 items each month in cities across the country to build the Consumer Price Index. 'Core' inflation drops food and energy, which swing, to see the trend. The Fed's 2 percent target is on a related index, PCE, which weights things differently.

slides.h: Inflation falling is not prices falling
slides.p: When inflation drops from 8 percent to 3, prices are still rising, just more slowly. Prices falling (deflation) is rare and usually a sign of a slump. People compare today's prices to a few years ago and feel the level; economists report the rate. Both are right about different things.

v.l1: level keeps rising as the rate slows

slides.p: The unemployment rate comes from a survey of about 60,000 households: you count as unemployed if you have no job and looked for one in the past four weeks. The 'jobs added' figure comes from a separate survey of about 120,000 employers. They're released together on the first Friday of the month and sometimes disagree.

b: counts jobs; one person can hold two

slides.p: People who stopped looking aren't unemployed; they're 'out of the labor force', along with students, retirees and carers. The labor-force participation rate (about 62 percent) tracks them. Broader measures (U-6) add discouraged and involuntary part-time workers and run several points higher than the headline.

items: U-6, incl. discouraged & part-time for economic reasons

slides.h: The Fed's two jobs and one tool
slides.p: The Federal Reserve is charged with maximum employment and stable prices. Its main tool is the federal funds rate, which sets the cost of overnight borrowing between banks and ripples into mortgages, car loans and business credit. Raising it cools demand and inflation; cutting it does the reverse, with a lag of a year or more.

slides.h: Reading the release without being fooled
slides.p: One month is noise; look at the three-month trend. Numbers get revised, often. Seasonal adjustment is why January layoffs don't show as a crash. A statistic that's good for the economy can be bad for you: GDP can grow while your wage doesn't. Check which number, which period, real or nominal, and whether it was revised.

items: Watch the revisions to prior months

quiz.q: If inflation falls from 8% to 3%, prices…
quiz.why: Inflation is a rate of change. Only deflation means prices actually fall, and that's rare.

quiz.q: Someone who gave up looking for work is counted as…
quiz.why: The headline rate counts only those who searched in the past four weeks; broader measures like U-6 include the discouraged.

quiz.q: The jobs-added number and the unemployment rate come from…
a: Two different surveys, of employers and of households
quiz.why: Payrolls come from about 120,000 employers; the rate from about 60,000 households. They can point different ways in a given month.

take: GDP counts final output; always ask real or nominal.
Inflation is a rate: falling inflation still means rising prices.
Unemployment counts active job seekers; payroll jobs come from a different survey. Watch trends and revisions.
